Acceptance summary:

This important resource paper describes a collection of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) produced from patients with a microdeletion of the 16p11.2 chromosomal locus, well-known to be associated with significant neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The work provides both a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process, as well as a plethora of information about changes in gene expression observed when neural progenitors are derived from these iPSCs. The results provided here, combined with the availability of these iPSCs from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative, should be useful to developmental neurobiologists, those interested in psychiatric disease, and, frankly, to anyone interested in large-scale iPSC-based disease modeling.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "16p11.2 CNV Imparts Transcriptional Alterations in Neural Development in an hiPSC Model of Corticogenesis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

The authors produced 65 iPSC clones from 13 individuals with CNVs at the 16p11.2 locus – 10 with microdeletions and 3 with microduplications. This locus is well-known to be associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The donor cells were provided by the Simons Foundation who also will make the iPSC clones available, making this a valuable cellular resource for those interested in this chromosomal locus and its role in brain development and function. The authors carried out a detailed analysis of the iPSC clones, produced using episomal reprogramming vectors, finding that many of the clones were compromised by unexpected, random integration of the reprogramming vectors with consequent effects on gene transcription in derived cells. The production of this large set of iPSC clones, as well as the cautionary tale concerning vector integration and a detailed RNAseq analysis of the integration-free clones make this paper, as a Tools and Resource publication, a valuable resource for the community.

Revisions for this paper:

We are mindful that additional experiments cannot be readily done at the moment. However, we believe that addressing some of these points, together with a reanalysis of the current data, will make this paper more useful to those interested in this area:

1) The data in this paper are restricted to iPSCs generated by episomal reprogramming. Since many, perhaps most, investigators are using Sendai virus, the authors should mention that point. Also do they conclude that episomal reprogramming should be avoided?

2) The analysis uses each clone a separate entity. As best as the reviewers can judge, 6 affected donors, not all of whom were diagnosed with ASD, 3 of which had 3 clones, 1 of which had 2 and the other 2 had 1 each, were used. There were also 3 unaffected donors (with 3, 2, and 2 clones). However, clones should not be weighted the same as individual donors. From Hoffman et al. Nat Comm 2017: "Due to the "repeated measures" study design where individuals are represented by multiple independent hiPSC-NPC and hiPSC-neuron lines, we used a linear mixed model by applying the duplicateCorrelation function in our limma/voom analysis. This approach is widely used to control the false positive rate in studies of repeated measures and its importance in hiPSC data sets was recently emphasized (citing Germain and Testa SCR 2017)". We recommend that the authors reanalyze their data so that each entry is a patient-associated value, rather than a clone-associated one.

3) Based on the results shown in this paper, it is a bit misleading to "strongly suggest" that "16p11.2 deletion may impact many functions important to neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric disease" – given that the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited and that no data of any observable phenotype was presented. It would be appropriate to tone down that statement and draw more conservative conclusions.

4) Unless the authors wish to include data for the duplication clones, The title "16p11.2 CNV imparts…" should be "16p11.2 microdeletion imparts…" since all duplication hiPSC clones in the analysis were excluded in the analysis steps of Figure 5 and 6.

5) QC questions:

a) Information on the controls is lacking in the main manuscript. Could the authors specifically clarify (in the Results or Materials and methods) the extent to which cases and controls are sex-, ethnicity- and age-matched, as well as whether they were reprogrammed together with the cases and by the same methods?

b) What was the polygenic risk score for the patients/controls? Might this have accounted for variable clinical presentations?

c) Were the hiPSCs karyotyped?

d) What QC was performed on RNAseq to confirm sample identity, cell type composition, etc? It would be helpful if the authors applied variance partition to uncover to what extent variation is explained by reprogramming method, genotype, donor, diagnosis, cell type, etc?

e) What is the Spearman's correlation coefficients for transcriptomic gene expression between donors and clones samples?

6) Questions involving additional useful data analysis

a) Integration with existing datasets and psychiatric genetic studies: Is there an enrichment of 16p11.2 DEGs for the GWAS loci for ASD, SZ or ADHD? Can the authors also test for enrichment of postmortem disease signatures as reported by the CommonMind Consortium, NIH HBCC and/or PsychEncode UCLA (Geschwind) analyses?

b) Are gene expression differences validated in existing 16p11.2 postmortem, hiPSC or mouse datasets (ie. PMID: 26829649)?

c) Given some recent discussions of convergence between CNV effects in psychiatric disease, are major findings from 16p11.2 conserved in hiPSC neuron datasets from other major CNVs (ie. 22q11.2 hiPSC PMID: 27846841 and mouse PMID: 29666363; 15q11.2 BioRxiv https://doi.org/10.1101/772541; NRXN1 PMID: 31784728)

d) Can the authors discuss whether they believe the genome-wide transcriptomic effects of 16p11.2 reflect chromatin loops between the CNV locus and other target genes? miR targets? Or downstream impacts of perturbed neuronal maturation/activity/signaling?

7) Are the authors able to comment on any phenotypic differences that they did observe between microdeletion lines and wt lines?

Revisions expected in follow-up work:

1) Characterization of micro-duplication lines.

2) Elaboration of phenotypic differences at the neural progenitor stage or in differentiated neurons.

results.result: The authors generated and characterized 65 hiPSC clones from 13 individuals with 16p11.2 CNVs (10 deletion donors, 3 duplication donors). The clones were validated for pluripotency, ploidy, genetic identity, and CNV breakpoints, and are publicly available through SFARI.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19-C36, C91, C97, C173, C175, C178, and C184 collectively document the generation, demographic characteristics, and quality control validation of the hiPSC resource. The data include immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, SNP array analysis, and functional differentiation assays that comprehensively validate the cell lines.

results.result: The authors successfully differentiated hiPSCs into cortical neural progenitor cells using a dual-SMAD inhibition protocol, generating neural rosettes with appropriate radial glial markers, polarity, and anterior cortical identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 describe the neural differentiation protocol and characterization with multiple validation methods including flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and RNA-seq analysis of patterning markers. The data demonstrate successful generation of cortical NPCs with appropriate cellular organization and regional identity.

results.result: The authors discovered that many hiPSC clones contained cryptically integrated episomal reprogramming vectors that caused widespread transcriptional alterations (3612 DE genes), developed a bioinformatic pipeline to detect plasmid integration and expression, and excluded integration-containing clones from subsequent analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C59 and C160-C172 document the discovery of plasmid integration through PCA, validation by qPCR/qRT-PCR, quantification of plasmid-derived transcripts, differential expression analysis showing 3612 affected genes, and development of a computational method to detect integration. The evidence includes multiple orthogonal validation approaches and functional analysis showing POU5F1 as the primary driver of transcriptional effects.

results.result: In integration-free 16p11.2 deletion NPCs, 14 of 56 genes in the 16p11.2 region were differentially expressed and downregulated in a copy-number-dependent manner, with a total of 107 DE genes identified (adjusted p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66, C101-C103, C105, C108, C185, and C186 describe the differential expression analysis with appropriate batch correction, statistical testing, qPCR validation, and consistency across individual clones. The finding that all 14 DE genes in the 16p11.2 region are downregulated is consistent with haploinsufficiency and supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Beyond the 16p11.2 region, 93 additional genes were differentially expressed in deletion NPCs, including genes enriched for ASD association and involved in neurodevelopmental processes such as synaptic function, MAPK signaling, cytoskeletal organization, and metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70, C114-C118, C187, and C188 describe gene ontology enrichment analysis showing significant enrichment for ASD-associated genes and neurodevelopmental pathways. The analysis is supported by DAVID enrichment, SFARI database queries, and functional categorization, though the authors appropriately note that some enrichments do not reach significance after multiple testing correction.

results.result: MAPK3 (encoding Erk1) was downregulated in all deletion lines and interacts with several other DE genes, supporting prior work implicating the Erk1/2 MAPK pathway in 16p11.2 phenotypes, though no changes in NPC proliferation were observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 and C123 describe the MAPK3 findings with RNA-seq, qPCR validation, and proliferation assays. The lack of proliferation phenotype is appropriately noted and consistent with prior work (Deshpande et al., 2017), suggesting MAPK3 effects may manifest at later developmental stages.

results.result: Four deletion clones contained additional CNVs outside the 16p11.2 region, but these did not significantly affect the average fold change of DE genes compared to other deletion clones.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 document additional CNVs and provide statistical analysis showing no significant difference in DE gene expression between clones with and without these additional CNVs. This appropriately addresses a potential confounding factor, though the analysis is limited by small sample size.

results.result: WGCNA identified 20 gene expression modules significantly associated with clinical traits in deletion patients, with modules correlating with both neurological and physical phenotypes but not containing genes that distinguish DEL from WT, suggesting patient-specific transcriptional programs contribute to phenotypic heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78, C132-C138, and C154-C157 describe the WGCNA analysis identifying trait-associated modules. The finding that these modules are distinct from DEL vs. WT differences is well-documented, though the interpretation regarding patient-specific etiology is appropriately presented as speculative.

results.result: GSEA of BMI-associated genes revealed enrichment for metabolic processes (69 gene sets), with the strongest enrichments in cell signaling pathways and responses to external stimuli, suggesting phenotypic variance involves both metabolic and signaling dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 and C139-C142 describe GSEA results with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.25) and functional categorization. The interpretation that both metabolic and signaling pathways contribute to phenotypic variance is supported by the enrichment data, though presented appropriately as hypothesis-generating.

results.result: The pink4 gene module showed high correlation with Weight Z-score, Language deficits, Age, and Head Circumference Z-score, containing genes involved in MAPK and Wnt signaling (FGF1, WIF1) and unexpectedly linking BMI and language phenotypes through shared gene programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87, C143-C146, and C148-C153 describe correlations between the pink4 module and multiple clinical traits. While the correlations are statistically significant, the mechanistic interpretations are highly speculative, and the unexpected association with Age (C152-C153) raises questions about confounding. The link between BMI and language phenotypes is novel but requires validation.

results.result: Genes related to later neurodevelopmental phenotypes (neurite branching, synapse development) are differentially expressed in early NPCs, with reduced KCTD13 and TAOK2 expression potentially impacting cortical network development and synaptic function.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122 and C124 connect early transcriptional changes to later phenotypes based on prior literature about KCTD13 and TAOK2 function. While the expression changes are well-documented, the causal link to later phenotypes is speculative and would require functional validation in more mature cell types.

results.result: Transcriptomic profiling identified alterations in gene expression patterns in early NPCs that precede morphological abnormalities at later stages, with disruptions in gene programs related to nervous system function and cellular metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C174, and C189 summarize the main findings connecting early transcriptional changes to later phenotypes and identifying metabolism as a key pathway. This is supported by the differential expression analysis, WGCNA, and GSEA results, though the temporal relationship to later phenotypes is inferred from comparison to prior literature rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: 16p11.2 CNVs are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (particularly ASD and SCZ), reciprocal neuroanatomical phenotypes (macro/microcephaly, brain volume changes), sensory processing abnormalities, and metabolic phenotypes (obesity/low BMI), as established by prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C18, C88-C90, and C92 summarize established knowledge about 16p11.2 CNVs from prior literature. These are appropriately cited background claims that provide context for the current study and are well-supported by the referenced literature.

results.result: The large hiPSC collection addresses methodological challenges in hiPSC modeling including clone-to-clone variability, epigenetic memory, and technical limitations of genetic engineering, providing opportunities to explore both CNV-specific effects and genetic background influences on phenotype penetrance.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96, C98-C99, and C179 describe the rationale and utility of the resource based on established knowledge about hiPSC variability and technical challenges. The statements are appropriately supported by citations and logical inference about the resource's value.

results.result: The authors emphasize the importance of screening for cryptic plasmid integration in episomally reprogrammed hiPSCs, noting these effects are most relevant for DNA-based reprogramming methods and could arise from either increased reprogramming factor expression or insertional mutagenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C159 and C162 provide methodological recommendations based on the integration findings. The recommendation is well-supported by the data showing widespread transcriptional effects, and the speculation about mechanisms (C162) is appropriately presented as hypothesis rather than conclusion.

results.result: The study aimed to identify which 16p11.2 genes are expressed in early cortical NPCs and show altered expression with deletion. Of 56 genes in the region, 15 are not expressed in NPCs and unlikely relevant for early patterning, while 41 expressed genes may have roles in early development, with 14 showing statistically significant downregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C104, C106-C107, and C109 describe the study objectives and interpretation of expression data. The inferences about developmental relevance based on expression levels are reasonable, though the speculation about genes with larger deletions (C104) is appropriately presented as uncertain.

results.result: DE genes suggest potential alterations in cell movement/locomotion, cytoskeletal organization, glucose metabolism, and proliferation through effects on structural genes (SELE, TEKT4, TUBGCP4, KLHL4), metabolic genes (TLCD3B, FBP2, ALDOA), and miRNAs (miR-301B, miR-637).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 make functional predictions based on gene ontology and prior literature about individual genes. While the expression changes are well-documented, the predicted cellular phenotypes are speculative and would require experimental validation. The miRNA findings are particularly uncertain given the RNA-seq protocol was not optimized for miRNA detection.

results.result: Patient-specific transcriptional abnormalities may interact with core 16p11.2 deficiency to generate heterogeneous phenotypes, with head circumference potentially linked to NPC proliferation abnormalities based on prior associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C131 and C147 propose a model for phenotypic heterogeneity based on WGCNA results and prior literature linking head circumference to NPC proliferation. While the model is plausible, it remains speculative without direct functional validation of the proposed interactions.

results.result: Prior work has shown morphological abnormalities in 16p11.2 neurons and transcriptional changes in idiopathic ASD NPCs, with widespread effects on NPC signaling pathways, but gene expression alterations in early 16p11.2 CNV neuroepithelial precursors had not been examined before this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C183 accurately summarize prior literature and identify the gap addressed by the current study. The citations appropriately support the statements about prior findings and the novelty of examining early NPCs in 16p11.2 CNV carriers.

results.result: The authors generated 65 hiPSC clones from 13 individuals with 16p11.2 CNVs (10 deletion, 3 duplication donors) using episomal reprogramming vectors. The clones were characterized for pluripotency, karyotype, identity, and CNV breakpoints, and are available through SFARI.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as 'a valuable cellular resource' and note that 'the production of this large set of iPSC clones' makes this 'a valuable resource for the community.' The acceptance summary describes this as 'an important resource paper' providing iPSCs that 'should be useful to developmental neurobiologists, those interested in psychiatric disease, and, frankly, to anyone interested in large-scale iPSC-based disease modeling.'

results.result: The hiPSC clones were successfully differentiated into cortical neural progenitor cells (NPCs) using a dual-SMAD inhibition protocol, forming neural rosettes with appropriate markers and anterior cortical identity, with no apparent differences between WT and CNV clones in rosette formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the neural differentiation characterization. The acceptance summary notes the paper provides 'information about changes in gene expression observed when neural progenitors are derived from these iPSCs,' implicitly accepting the differentiation protocol and characterization.

results.result: Many hiPSC clones contained unexpected random integration of episomal reprogramming vectors, particularly POU5F1, which caused widespread transcriptional effects (>3600 DE genes). The authors developed a bioinformatic pipeline to detect plasmid integration and expression, and excluded integration-containing clones from subsequent analyses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as 'a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process' and note that 'the cautionary tale concerning vector integration' makes this paper valuable. Reviewers request clarification about whether episomal reprogramming should be avoided and note the relevance to Sendai virus methods, but do not challenge the findings themselves.

results.result: After excluding integration-containing clones, insufficient duplication clones remained (n=4) for analysis, so subsequent transcriptomic analyses focused exclusively on deletion clones from six individuals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note this limitation, requesting that 'The title "16p11.2 CNV imparts…" should be "16p11.2 microdeletion imparts…" since all duplication hiPSC clones in the analysis were excluded.' This indicates acceptance of the sample limitation while requesting appropriate framing.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis of integration-free deletion NPCs identified 107 differentially expressed genes compared to WT, including 14 downregulated genes within the 16p11.2 locus (validated by qPCR) and 93 genes outside the deletion interval.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise significant methodological concerns, stating 'clones should not be weighted the same as individual donors' and recommending reanalysis using linear mixed models to properly account for repeated measures. They note 'the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited' and request more conservative conclusions. The finding is not rejected but requires methodological revision.

results.result: The differentially expressed genes are enriched for neuropsychiatric disease functions and ASD-associated genes (including CNTNAP2), and include genes relevant to synaptic function, MAPK signaling, and neuroepithelial development.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge these enrichment analyses, they request additional validation: 'Is there an enrichment of 16p11.2 DEGs for the GWAS loci for ASD, SZ or ADHD?' and 'Are gene expression differences validated in existing 16p11.2 postmortem, hiPSC or mouse datasets?' This suggests the enrichment findings need external validation to be fully supported.

results.result: MAPK3 (Erk1) and TAOK2 from the 16p11.2 region were downregulated across deletion lines. Despite MAPK3 downregulation, no changes in NPC proliferation were observed, consistent with prior work. The authors suggest these genes may impact cortical network development and synaptic function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the lack of observable phenotype, stating 'no data of any observable phenotype was presented' and that it is 'misleading to "strongly suggest" that "16p11.2 deletion may impact many functions important to neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric disease"' given the limited evidence. They request the authors 'tone down that statement and draw more conservative conclusions.'

results.result: WGCNA identified 123 gene expression modules, with 20 showing significant associations with clinical variables. The pink4 module showed strong correlations with Age, Weight Z-score, Height Z-score, Head Circumference Z-score, and Language traits.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise concerns about the statistical approach, recommending reanalysis with proper accounting for donor-level effects rather than treating clones as independent. They also request additional QC: 'What QC was performed on RNAseq to confirm sample identity, cell type composition, etc? It would be helpful if the authors applied variance partition to uncover to what extent variation is explained by reprogramming method, genotype, donor, diagnosis, cell type, etc?'

results.result: GSEA of BMI-associated genes identified enrichment for metabolic processes, signaling pathways, and gene expression regulation, with the strongest enrichments in cellular processes and signaling pathways related to cell responses to external stimuli.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge these findings, the methodological concerns about clone-level vs. donor-level analysis apply equally to this WGCNA-based result. The request to reanalyze with proper statistical models suggests these correlations need validation with appropriate methods.

results.result: The pink4 module's correlation with both Weight Z-score and Language suggests a novel link between BMI and language phenotypes in 16p11.2 deletion. Module genes include MAPK and Wnt pathway components (FGF1, WIF1), and correlations involve insulin signaling genes, AMIGO1, and KCNMB4.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not directly address these specific correlations but their general concern about overstated conclusions applies. They note 'it is a bit misleading to "strongly suggest"' functional impacts 'given that the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited and that no data of any observable phenotype was presented.' The speculative nature of linking NPCs to BMI phenotypes requires more conservative framing.

results.result: The WGCNA results suggest that patient-specific transcriptional programs independent of the 16p11.2 deletion may contribute to phenotypic heterogeneity, with some correlations involving genes outside the deletion interval and BMI-associated changes detected even in neural progenitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request clarification about polygenic risk scores: 'What was the polygenic risk score for the patients/controls? Might this have accounted for variable clinical presentations?' This indicates the interpretation of patient-specific effects needs additional genetic context. The speculative nature of these claims requires more conservative conclusions as requested by reviewers.

results.result: Four deletion clones contained additional CNVs (14q11.1 deletion, 14q11.2 duplication, 7p11.2 deletion) potentially associated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but these did not significantly affect the average fold change of DE genes and are unlikely to account for the reported transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this analysis. The documentation of additional CNVs addresses their QC concern about background genetic variation, and the statistical comparison showing no significant effect supports the authors' conclusion that these CNVs don't confound the main findings.

results.result: The transcriptional alterations in NPCs precede morphological abnormalities reported at later neurodevelopmental stages, suggesting early transcriptomic perturbations may act as priming events for later functional alterations in more mature cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers challenge this interpretation, noting 'no data of any observable phenotype was presented' and requesting the authors 'tone down that statement and draw more conservative conclusions.' They list as 'Revisions expected in follow-up work: Elaboration of phenotypic differences at the neural progenitor stage or in differentiated neurons,' indicating this claim requires additional experimental support.

results.result: The authors emphasize the importance of screening for cryptic plasmid integration when using episomal reprogramming, noting these effects are most relevant for DNA-based methods and less likely for RNA-based methods like Sendai virus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly request discussion of this point: 'Since many, perhaps most, investigators are using Sendai virus, the authors should mention that point. Also do they conclude that episomal reprogramming should be avoided?' This indicates reviewers view this as an important cautionary message that needs clarification rather than challenging the underlying finding.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on hiPSC resource generation and characterization (C3, C19-C36, C91, C97, C173, C175, C178, C184). Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED as a valuable community resource with comprehensive validation.
Perfect agreement on neural differentiation protocol and NPC characterization (C37-C45). Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED; peer reviewers implicitly accept by not challenging the methods.

Strong agreement on plasmid integration findings (C46-C58, C160-C172). Both find this SUPPORTED as an important cautionary tale. Peer reviewers request clarification about episomal methods but do not challenge the core findings.
Perfect agreement on additional CNVs analysis (C73-C76). Both find this SUPPORTED; peer reviewers accept that additional CNVs don't confound main findings.

Agreement on GSEA results (C79-C82, C139-C142) but with methodological concerns. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to clone vs. donor statistical issues requiring reanalysis.
Agreement on methodological recommendations about integration (C158-C159). Both find this SUPPORTED; peer reviewers explicitly request discussion of implications for Sendai virus methods.

Disagreement on differential expression analysis (C60-C66, C101-C103, C105, C108, C185-C186). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising significant concerns about treating clones as independent samples and requesting linear mixed models.
Agreement on sample limitation (C59, C101). Both acknowledge that duplication clones were excluded; peer reviewers request title change to reflect focus on microdeletion only.
Disagreement on gene ontology enrichment (C67-C70, C114-C118). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting external validation against GWAS loci and existing datasets.

Disagreement on MAPK3 findings and functional implications (C110-C113, C121-C124). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting lack of observable phenotype and requesting more conservative conclusions.

Agreement on uncertainty of clinical trait correlations (C83-C87, C143-C146, C148-C153). Both rate UNCERTAIN; OpenEval notes speculative interpretations while peer reviewers request more conservative framing given limited phenotypic data.

Partial overlap on WGCNA analysis (C77-C78, C132-C133). OpenEval finds trait-associated modules SUPPORTED while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting reanalysis with proper donor-level statistical models and variance partitioning.

Overlap on WGCNA module interpretation (C137-C138, C154-C157). OpenEval finds patient-specific effects SUPPORTED but speculative; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN and request polygenic risk score analysis to contextualize variable presentations.
Partial overlap on WGCNA clinical correlations (C83-C85). Both note methodological concerns; peer reviewers emphasize need for proper statistical accounting of donor vs. clone effects.

Disagreement on linking early changes to later phenotypes (C120-C124). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN noting speculation; peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN and explicitly request more conservative conclusions given no observable phenotype.
Overlap on functional predictions (C120). Both rate UNCERTAIN; peer reviewers note lack of phenotypic data undermines strong functional claims.

Disagreement on main conclusions (C5-C6, C174, C189). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with caveats about temporal inference; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting tone down of conclusions and noting no observable phenotype was presented.
Agreement on uncertainty of phenotypic heterogeneity model (C131, C147). Both rate UNCERTAIN; peer reviewers request polygenic risk score context for variable clinical presentations.
OpenEval finds background literature claims (C1-C2, C7-C18, C88-C90, C92) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation; these are contextual citations not directly evaluated by reviewers.
OpenEval finds rationale and resource utility claims (C93-C96, C98-C99, C179) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation; reviewers focus on empirical findings rather than rationale.
OpenEval finds study objectives and expression interpretation (C100, C104, C106-C107, C109) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation of these framing claims.

OpenEval rates functional predictions from gene ontology (C125-C130) as UNCERTAIN, noting need for experimental validation especially for miRNA findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation of these specific predictions.
OpenEval finds literature summary and gap identification (C180-C183) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation; these are background claims establishing novelty.
